overview.text: Influenza viruses, commonly called flu viruses, are contagious respiratory viruses that infect the nose, throat, and lungs. They belong to the Orthomyxoviridae family and carry their genetic information as segmented, single-stranded RNA. Four types—A, B, C, and D—are recognized; types A and B cause seasonal epidemics in people, while influenza A is the only type known to cause flu pandemics. Influenza A is notable for its changing surface proteins: hemagglutinin (H) helps the virus attach to cells, and neuraminidase (N) helps newly formed viruses leave infected cells. A subtype name such as H1N1 identifies the virus’s H and N versions. Flu spreads mainly in respiratory droplets.

key_facts.text: Influenza A and B cause seasonal epidemics in people; influenza A is the only type known to cause flu pandemics.
Influenza A subtypes are named by combining their hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) types, as in H1N1; 18 H and 11 N subtypes are recognized.
Influenza A and B viruses have genomes made of eight separate RNA segments.
Hemagglutinin binds to a cell receptor, while neuraminidase helps new viruses release from an infected cell.
Flu spreads mainly through droplets produced when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks; spread from contaminated surfaces is less common.
